crash-reporter: c++iza anomaly detector and have it use the journal Have anomaly_detector use the systemd journal as its log source instead of reading from /var/log/messages. Audit messages have been moved to /var/log/audit/audit.log, and attempts to make anomaly_detector read two files proved complicated: https://crrev.com/c/1630336 It was cleaner to completely rewrite anomaly detector by migrating it to C++ than to try to fit the current unit tests with the journal implementation. This has the added advantage of reducing the dependencies of the unit test and making it much faster since we no longer need to repeatedly call sleep. It's also now understood by the unit test framework as a group of multiple tests instead of one big test. Reading from journal has several advantages, most of which we aren't taking advantage of in this change, but can done in the future. Possible future improvements: * Use sd_journal_add_match and friends to make following the journal more efficient. * Save the journal cursor between boots to avoid missing certain early-boot and shutdown crashes: https://crbug.com/343954#c8 * Leverage structured audit data. Journald actually has all the audit fields we parse from the audit line as structured data. Use these instead of parsing the audit line. vm_tools: Make X sommelier scale internal displays differently X11 applications historically use DPI to decide their scaling, however this does not work for laptops, which are closer to you and so usually have a higher DPI. To solve this problem, the X server usually lies about the DPI of laptops. We emulate this behaviour for chromeos by applying a scale factor if the display is the internal one. We choose 0.66 semi-arbitrarily (based on measuring sample laptop/desktop screen distances in our office). Whilst this fixes some devices, it breaks others, base on a pre-existing bug in sommelier where it would choose a DPI bucket that is no higher than the true DPI. E.g. the pixelbook2's DPI of 232 would be rounded to 160 (not 240) which looks correct, because we werent applying the laptop-distance scale, whereas another device's 168 DPI would be rounded to 160, which looks unusually big (96 would be better), because we werent applying the laptop-distance factor which means the "ideal" DPI for that device is actually 112, closer to 96. sane-backends: Disable non-USB drivers By default, sane-backends includes drivers for a bunch of SCSI, parallel port, and serial port scanners. Since Chrome OS devices don't have the needed ports to plug these in, we can save ~3MB on the rootfs by omitting these drivers. To get the list of drivers that don't support USB, I took a list of all the files from /etc/sane.d that didn't mention usb and then double-checked against their man pages.
